x86-64 floating-register storage follow-up (EK619): the selected `QueryTaskTagList.c` reports a 10-byte floating register through `TaskTag_REG_FloatSize` but assigns a full 16-byte `MMReg` to the caller's output for an accepted indexed floating tag. `arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpucontext.h` defines the 10 data bytes and six padding bytes. A direct client sizing its buffer from the reported value can receive a six-byte overrun; no selected in-tree indexed-float caller was found. The general-register count of 15 matches the contiguous `rax` through `rbp` saved fields, so no separate count mismatch was credited. No query was run.

I/O publication follow-up (EK8799): reread the complete `ReplyMsg`, `CheckIO`, `WaitIO`, `SendIO`, `DoIO`, `GetMsg`, and `InternalPutMsg` paths. `SendIO` and `DoIO` reset a reused request's node type before invoking `BeginIO` (`rom/exec/sendio.c:48-56`; `rom/exec/doio.c:53-70`), but that does not close the interval where `ReplyMsg` has changed the type to `NT_REPLYMSG` and `InternalPutMsg` has not linked it (`replymsg.c:60-64`; `putmsg.c:83-92`). For the selected timer-interrupt callers, their owner task must run on another CPU to observe this interval; a task-context reply producer could be preempted on one CPU, but no selected task-context polling pair was established in this pass. No concurrent I/O was run.

EK8799 asynchronous I/O producer census addition (2026-10-17): checked the optional USB Mass Storage device's slow-command path. `dev_BeginIO` clears `IOF_QUICK` and queues the request to the unit worker (`workbench/devs/USB/classes/MassStorage/storage_device.c:697-728`); the selected storage worker dequeues it, handles it, and calls `ReplyMsg` from task context (`storage_task.c:232-251`). This confirms another selected task-context producer can be preempted between the `NT_REPLYMSG` store and reply-port insertion on a single CPU. I found no maintained in-tree client pair that both targets this device and polls or calls `WaitIO` in that interval, so this is corroborating producer evidence, not a new in-tree trigger or separate finding. External device clients remain within EK8799's public API scope. No device I/O was run.

Break caller follow-up for other-drivers OD1652: the selected shell command's `NAME` search can match the console worker's `TASKTAG_NAME` of `console.device`, and the command defaults to `SIGBREAKF_CTRL_C` before calling `Signal` (`workbench/c/Break.c:156-188,193-220`; `rom/devs/console/console.c:107-114`). The worker explicitly exits on that signal without unregistering its input handler (`rom/devs/console/consoletask.c:237-251,492-496`). This selected caller strengthens the driver trigger; it does not change the existing Exec-specific Break findings. No command or worker shutdown was run.

x86-64 Exec vector recheck (EK494 withdrawn): `NewStackSwap` calls `Disable` through public Exec vector 20 at offset -160 after `entry` returns. The x86-64 CPU header enables `UseExecstubs`, the generated assembly header emits the `UseExecstubs` define, the selected architecture manifest includes `execstubs.s`, and that stub pushes and pops `%rax` around the internal C `Disable` call (`arch/x86_64-all/include/aros/cpu.h:151-158`; `compiler/include/asm.c:235-236`; `arch/x86_64-all/exec/mmakefile.src:21-35`; `arch/x86_64-all/exec/execstubs.s:25-57,105-110`). The generic C body is not the direct public vector and does not establish a clobbered return, so the report entry is withdrawn and cross-architecture comparison rows corrected. Generated assembly and a swapped call were not run; other stack and optional-argument contracts remain pending.

Reply-publication follow-up (EK8799): the complete `ReplyMsg`, `InternalPutMsg`, `CheckIO` and `WaitIO` bodies were rechecked against selected lan78xx and Poseidon PoPo timer loops. `ReplyMsg` stores `NT_REPLYMSG` before `InternalPutMsg` disables interrupts, takes the reply-port spinlock and links the node (`rom/exec/replymsg.c:60-64`; `putmsg.c:78-96`). Both clients test `CheckIO`, call `WaitIO`, and resubmit the same timer request (`rom/usb/classes/lan78xx/lan78xx.class.c:628-638`; `rom/usb/poseidon/popo.gui.c:284-291`). A client that runs in the store-to-link interval can have `WaitIO` remove an unlinked node. Their normal single-task loops do not themselves create that overlap; for these timer-IRQ producers, the selected route requires execution on another CPU while the reply is being published. Task-context ReplyMsg callers may have a uniprocessor preemption window, but no such selected client was established in this follow-up. The previously suspected Intuition route uses a private reply port and stack timerequest, and input.device queues the two nonquick settings commands to its priority-20 worker (`rom/intuition/setprefs.c:110-164`; `rom/devs/input/input.c:149-173`; `rom/devs/input/input_intern.h:44`; `rom/devs/input/processevents.c:417-433`), but synchronous DoIO/WaitIO blocks until the reply-port signal after insertion, so that route is excluded. The reset-callback/C:Wait independent-signal callers and conditional lan78xx/PoPo cross-CPU polling paths remain the selected observer evidence. No separate lan78xx or PoPo defect is credited beyond EK8799, and no concurrent schedule was run.

Pthread detach/worker-exit interleaving follow-up (EK569): the selected `pthread_detach` store and worker's final `if (!inf->detached)` were reread together. Detach after completion and detach after the worker has chosen its joinable branch both leave a detached, nonnull task slot that `pthread_join` rejects and the library exit hook waits on. These are two timings of EK569's same lifecycle defect, so no duplicate candidate was added. No overlapping lifecycle calls were run.

Pthread creation-failure slot follow-up (EK609): the full selected `pthread_create` failure return was traced against `GetThreadId(NULL)` and later join/cancel validation. A failed `CreateNewProcTags` leaves a null task pointer, releases `thread_sem`, then checks and clears its slot outside the lock. A second creator can repopulate that slot in the gap, so the first can invalidate the second record or mistake its worker for a successful creation. No allocation/process failure or concurrent creation was run; wider worker-start contracts remain pending.

Pthread join cancellation follow-up (EK608): `pthread_join` tests cancellation only before waiting for CTRL-F; deferred `pthread_cancel` sends CTRL-C, which Exec `Wait` does not accept in that mask. A joiner blocked on an unfinished worker therefore stays asleep after cancellation, and a later successful join does not process the pending request. Self-join and simultaneous joiner contracts were examined but not assigned separate candidates; external clients and runtime behavior remain pending.

Named pthread semaphore lifetime follow-up (EK607): the complete public `semaphore.h` and selected `semaphore.c` body were compared with the active link-library manifest. `sem_close` has no reference bookkeeping, while `sem_unlink` frees the object returned by prior `sem_open` calls. A waiter may be asleep with the embedded mutex released; `sem_destroy` then ignores `pthread_cond_destroy`'s busy result and lets unlink free its condition. This is part of EK607's valid named-handle lifetime problem, not a separate claim that standalone `sem_destroy` is safe with active waiters. No selected in-tree client or runtime execution was found. The header, module configuration, README and debug helper read this turn are tracked below; external clients and the remaining semaphore contracts stay pending.

Pthread semaphore initialization follow-up: `sem_init` discards its `pthread_mutex_init` and `pthread_cond_init` results (`compiler/pthread/semaphore.c:154-169`), but it first rejects a null `sem`, and both selected callees, with the null attributes supplied here, only initialize embedded Exec semaphore/list state and return zero (`compiler/pthread/pthread_mutex_init.c:26-47`; `compiler/pthread/pthread_cond_init.c:26-50`). Thus those ignored return values do not establish an allocation-failure defect for this selected path. `sem_wait` passes a null deadline to `sem_timedwait`, which reaches the condition wait without opening a timer device (`semaphore.c:226-265`; `pthread_cond_timedwait.c:49-65,124-145`); timer-opening failures belong only to timed waits. No new semaphore candidate credited from these checks; external API clients and pshared semantics remain pending.

Pthread barrier cycle follow-up: `pthread_barrier_init`, `pthread_barrier_wait` and `pthread_barrier_destroy` were reread together (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:434-519`) against their embedded mutex/condition layout and `PTHREAD_BARRIER_FLAG` (`pthread.h:351-371`; `pthread_intern.h:84`). For ordinary counts below the flag, the last entrant publishes the release generation and broadcasts; each prior waiter decrements the exit count, and the next entrant waits until it returns to the flag. Destroy checks for exiting threads and then checks the condition's waiter list through `pthread_cond_destroy`; a waiting pre-release thread is not silently accepted by that path. No selected in-tree `pthread_barrier_*` call was found outside definitions and commented POSIXC config entries. Caller lifetime, unusual large counts and attr/pshared semantics remain open; no barrier candidate added from this cycle check.

Pthread barrier cancellation follow-up (EK625): both `pthread_barrier_wait` condition waits retain `barrier->lock` through the call (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:476-519`). `_pthread_cond_timedwait` reacquires that lock and removes its waiter before `pthread_testcancel` exits the thread on the cancellation signal (`compiler/pthread/pthread_cond_timedwait.c:140-169`; `pthread.c:961-975`), so the barrier wrapper never reaches its unlock. A later participant stalls on the internal lock. This extends EK625's same cancellation-cleanup defect from `sem_wait`; no in-tree barrier client or runtime cancellation was found. Other barrier lifetime and API contracts remain open.

Pthread static read-write-lock follow-up (EK606): the full 638-line public header was read against the previously reviewed `pthread.c` lock operations and Exec `InitSemaphore`. All selected read/write acquisition variants can reinitialize a static lock after another CPU has acquired it because the invalidity check has no one-time claim. The header row below now reflects the full read. No selected in-tree static rwlock instance or concurrent execution was found; external clients, other pthread contracts and runtime behavior remain pending.

Signal-allocation caller follow-up: the complete `AllocSignal`, `FreeSignal`, `CreateMsgPort`, `DeleteMsgPort` and `Wait` bodies were rechecked against SonixcamTool's completed-frame path (`rom/usb/shellapps/SonixcamTool.c:820-823,1230-1238,151-155`). `AllocSignal(-1)` returns `-1` only after the task's allocation mask is full (`rom/exec/allocsignal.c:79-102`); `CreateMsgPort` has already allocated and checked its own distinct bit (`rom/exec/createmsgport.c:50-74`). SonixcamTool therefore can proceed with a valid message port but no image-completion bit, as other-driver OD1720 records. `FreeSignal(-1)` is explicitly harmless (`rom/exec/freesignal.c:27-29,48-56`), so the teardown call is not a second defect. This is caller misuse of Exec's documented failure result rather than a new allocator finding. No signal-exhaustion run was performed; other public callers remain pending.

PC frequency-governor caller recheck (EK597): the selected `arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_freq.c` and x86-64 `kernel_cpu.c` bodies were traced from APIC load sampling through `core_CPUFreqInit`, AMD P-state discovery, target selection and the MSR setter. A valid enabled P-state index zero is treated as a missing maximum, causing high and low load thresholds to program the same highest enabled index when more than one P-state exists. The software current-target field also records the unclamped 0xff high-load value. Intel ratio handling and real hardware clock effects remain separate contracts; no MSR was accessed during review.

POSIX descriptor caller follow-up (EK594–EK596): selected `compiler/crt/posixc/fcntl.c` was read in full against the descriptor-table helper, open-mode conversion, public flag definitions and DOS `ChangeMode` forwarding. F_SETFL always constructs mode -1, F_GETFL omits access-mode bits, and F_DUPFD passes a negative minimum into an unchecked descriptor-array index. The 217-line caller body is tracked below; only the relevant `__fdesc.c` helper ranges were read, so that file remains targeted rather than fully audited. Two rows were added. No descriptor operation was run.

Named-semaphore caller follow-up (EK588-EK592): selected `compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c` was added as an Exec semaphore dependency after reading its complete body and `compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:78,343-347`. Its first-use Find/Add pair is under local-CPU `Forbid` rather than one cross-CPU publication lock, allowing duplicate named file locks on SMP; its globally shared `file_locks` list has unprotected AddHead/traversal/removal; and its library init hook applies `NEWLIST` to an unchecked `AllocMem` result. These are posixc caller defects recorded in the Exec/kernel report because they directly use Exec's public semaphore and allocation contracts; EK876's distinct FindSemaphore lifetime gap remains. Three dependency rows were added below; final descriptor close does not release an acquired lock (EK591), and failed record allocation is ignored after acquisition (EK592). Final-close behavior is covered by EK591; descriptor duplication, path aliasing, and generated base-copy lifetime remain pending; no flock execution was run.

M68K ViewPort shadow follow-up (EK582): selected `ViewPortAddress` returns a screen-owned ViewPort (`rom/intuition/viewportaddress.c:15-53`), whose RasInfo/BitMap and ColorMap are initialized on successful screen opening (`rom/intuition/openscreen.c:1363-1382,1406-1411`). The generated thunk at `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:5313-5321` makes a ViewPort shadow. Its ColorMap and RasInfo entries in `m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:3969-3981` have type zero and no sub-layout, so `m68kemu_shadow.c:48-77` writes guest zero absent a matching type-zero shadow. Pthread CRT-hook lifetime follow-up: the complete selected 222-line `compiler/crt/posixc/__threadhook.c` body was read against `compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:63-91,134,201`. The registry allocation is published through Exec's semaphore list and is never removed or freed by the checked source; posixc expunge removes its static callback node under the registry semaphore. This rules out a freed registry structure from normal posixc expunge. Pthread snapshots callback function pointers, drops that semaphore and then invokes them; whether the library can expunge between snapshot and call depends on open-count ownership across active worker startup/exit and remains unproved. No separate candidate was added from this gap. Selected build manifest paths and task-storage publication remain subject to their existing findings; no worker or expunge sequence was run.

Pthread scheduler-caller follow-up (EK833): the selected `compiler/pthread/sched.c` body was read against `rom/exec/settaskpri.c`, `reschedule.c` and `enable.c`. In the non-`__AMIGA__` branch used by the AROS path, `sched_yield` changes its own priority to -10 and back; the self-comparison in `SetTaskPri` schedules neither transition. The selected `pthread_spin_lock` retry loop calls this function after every failed test-and-set (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:758-778`), so contention can spin until a scheduler event lands while the temporary priority is still active; `SetTaskPri` re-enables interrupts before returning, making that interval possible but not guaranteeing a handoff. The alternative Amiga/MorphOS branch explicitly requests a switch. Rechecked the scheduler interval: `SetTaskPri` calls `Enable` before returning, so a timer interrupt can preempt while the spin waiter still has priority -10; if the owner priority is above -10, PC `core_Schedule` can then switch to it. If a quantum switch occurs after the old priority is restored, the spinner is requeued ahead of the lower-priority owner (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:107-134,201-227`; `rom/exec/enqueue.c:70-97`). Thus the defect is lack of a requested voluntary handoff; progress can depend on a timer landing in the temporary-priority interval, and persistent starvation is conditional on timing and priorities. The selected link-library build adds `-D__AROS__` (`config/make.tmpl:2642`), and AROS GCC specs do not define `__AMIGA__` (`config/specs.in:26`); external flags and runtime contention remain open. This extends EK833 without adding a separate finding.

Public-port and I/O-request recheck: the complete selected `AddPort`, `CreateMsgPort`, `DeleteMsgPort`, `FindPort`, `RemPort`, `CreateIORequest` and `DeleteIORequest` bodies were reread together. The port list mutations pair their SMP lock, while `FindPort` releases its read lock before returning a borrowed pointer; selected GfxControl and ConClip paths have caller-specific coverage in GD4286, GD4019 and OD806; other public-port callers remain open. `DeleteMsgPort` frees the signal in the deleting task and does not drain pending replies, so cross-task deletion and outstanding-message ownership remain caller contracts. The request pair still truncates the allocated byte count into `UWORD mn_Length` (EK326); the selected M68K bridge forwards a guest-supplied size, and its separate shadow-allocation failure is already EK408. No additional Exec candidate was retained from these seven bodies; broader callers remain open.

Forbid cross-CPU caller follow-up (OD1602): selected Poseidon `pLockSemExcl`, `pLockSemShared` and `pUnlockSem` use `Forbid` as their only protection around custom semaphore owner/count/list transitions (`rom/usb/poseidon/poseidon.library.c:492-675`). Exec's own `Forbid` contract says it only prevents local-CPU task switches on SMP and requires an additional spinlock for parallel data (`rom/exec/forbid.c:55-66`). This is a Poseidon caller defect, recorded in the other-drivers report, rather than a new Exec candidate. Other Forbid clients remain pending.

Message-port signal follow-up (OD1598): Exec `PutMsg` appends under the port spinlock and dispatches `PA_SIGNAL` using `1 << mp_SigBit` after unlocking (`rom/exec/putmsg.c:83-106`); `WaitPort` likewise forms a mask from that bit (`rom/exec/waitport.c:63-95`). Poseidon's selected hardware task leaves two failed `AllocSignal` results unchecked in those byte-sized fields and uses them in its own wait mask (`rom/usb/poseidon/poseidon.library.c:9157-9173,9247-9296`). The invalid producer state is recorded as other-driver OD1598, not a separate Exec defect. PA_CALL dispatch and wider port-lifetime contracts remain pending.

Port callback caller follow-up: selected `rom/usb/poseidon/poseidon.library.c:9153-9173,9248-9255` uses numeric `PA_CALLBACK = 3`, which is Exec's `PA_CALL` branch in `rom/exec/putmsg.c:119-130`, when a USB controller advertises `UHCF_QUICKIO`. A repository search found the in-tree PCI USB/xHCI capability writes only under `PCIUSB_QUICKIO`, with no in-repository definition of that build option (`rom/usb/pciusb/uhwcmd.c:580-583`; `rom/usb/pcixhci/uhwcmd.c:589-592`). The optional m68k Deneb target unconditionally advertises QuickIO (`arch/m68k-amiga/usb/denebusb/uhwcmd.c:782-791`; its manifest selects that body); OD1644 records the resulting D0/A1 callback-register mismatch. PCI USB/xHCI still need the nondefault build option. Poseidon's callback drains its port directly with `RemHead` outside the port spinlock; any concurrent QuickIO callback issue belongs to the driver/USB-stack review, while Exec's general PA_CALL reentrancy and callback lifetime contracts remain pending. No QuickIO or SMP callback run was performed.

A direct-call sweep checked selected `font.datatype` `SNPrintf` aliases: both destinations are in `MEMF_CLEAR` allocations, so their OOM result remains a valid empty string and adds no unterminated-buffer consequence. `workbench/devs/diskimage/device/unit.c` also calls `VSNPrintf`, but its local MetaMake target has no parent in the current `workbench-devs-complete` aggregate and remains within the 438 untracked workbench/devs raw-gap paths; its public `UnitControl` caller separately initializes the error buffer and preserves the error code, so it was not credited as an active selected trigger. A repository-wide symbol/call census found the selected font.datatype calls, the utility test, diskimage callers, and CAMD’s `mysprintf` wrapper. CAMD expands `mysprintf` to `SNPrintf` only under `__amigaos4__`; the AROS path uses its local `RawDoFmt` implementation (`workbench/libs/camd/camd_intern.h:387-392`; `strings.c:38-49`), so those calls are not selected VSNPrintf callers here. Both font.datatype destinations are in MEMF_CLEAR allocations (workbench/classes/datatypes/font/otag.c:191-198; fontclass.c:518-531), so VSNPrintf allocation failure leaves a valid empty string there and adds no selected caller defect. The utility test is not production; diskimage has no parent in the current workbench-devs-complete aggregate and remains outside this selected-caller claim. External clients of the public API and actual memory-pressure behavior remain open. |

| `compiler/crt/posixc/__fdesc.c` | Full body and descriptor ownership caller recheck; broader synchronization pending | Descriptor ownership lookup, fd.library hooks, slot publication/growth, mode conversion, open/create/error unwinding, pooled descriptor allocation/free, standard streams, vfork table copy, OpenLib/CloseLib lifecycle, close-on-exec and stdio handoff were read. EK9120 follows dup2() large-target growth through 32-bit allocation-size wrap and inflated slot-count publication. EK594–EK596 use `__oflags2amode`, stored open flags and the unchecked negative `__getfirstfd` index. EK598 follows both `__getfdesc` foreign ownership and `__getfdslot`'s failure to vacate a socket target. EK599 follows `__copy_fdarray` skipping a closed parent stdin and `__init_fd` dereferencing the resulting null child slot under EXEC_PARENT; a partial copy failure can do the same. Selected `__open` calls come from open and freopen; a failed freopen may close its prior descriptor during slot replacement, which does not by itself establish a distinct contract violation. `stderrlogic` passes a possible failed NIL: handle to SetVBuf, but DOS SetVBuf returns EOF on null rather than dereferencing it. EK600 is detailed in the report: partial vfork descriptor-copy failure after FCB reference increments reaches generated OpenLib rollback, which does not invoke CLOSELIB and loses the copied descriptors and pool. Vfork snapshot follow-up: the child `__init_fd` passes the parent's raw `fd_array` and slot count to `__copy_fdarray`, whose source traversal is not protected by the parent `fd_sem` (`__fdesc.c:692-718,765-776`); a concurrent parent descriptor-table grow could free that source array. The child setup runs while the vfork caller waits and independently-created worker Tasks continue (`__vfork.c:488-527`). However, the only identified table mutators are open/close paths, and both public APIs state they must not be used in a threaded application (`open.c:59-64`; `close.c:36-38`); no selected supported caller mutating the parent's table in that window was established, so this interleaving is retained as an unsupported-client boundary rather than a finding. The worker's stored `fd_owner` remains the parent base while that base temporarily redirects its own owner for pretend-child execution (`__threadhook.c:190-219`; `__vfork.c:552-570,607-620`). EK10313 follows explicit dup2 into a local-empty slot globally owned by another POSIXC process: __getfdslot skips FD_Reserve based only on the shared owner class, and __setfdesc overwrites its global data pointer; a later close can free the reservation while the other local descriptor remains. The fd.library allocator can then reuse the number for a socket, making the surviving local POSIXC descriptor route through the wrong hooks. The same-owner skip is intended for vfork-inherited entries, but does not establish that the global owner belongs to this process. The direct-call census found `dup`/`F_DUPFD` select globally free slots; hosted logging, the DBus test, and Apple-only WirelessManager use standard streams, while minires replaces a socket descriptor. No checked-in selected caller exercises a cross-process target collision. The public `dup2()` contract nevertheless permits the separate-process case (its own NOTES prohibit shared-library and threaded use only), and the local-table/global-owner mismatch is now promoted as EK10313. Shared DOS-handle safety across tasks and broader FCB synchronization remain open. Lookup recheck: `__getfdesc` releases the owner `fd_sem` before returning a borrowed `fdesc`; a same-number concurrent close can then free the descriptor before read/write/fcntl use. `close.c:37-38` explicitly says close must not be used in a threaded application, and the selected API does not establish a supported concurrent-close path, so this is not promoted. `__dos64_read/write` do hold the FCB I/O semaphore once reached; that does not pin the earlier descriptor pointer. EK8994/EK8995 now cover the `pipe()` allocation-failure and concurrent slot-publication paths that use this table; ordinary `open()`/`close()` calls remain explicitly documented as unsupported in threaded applications. Vfork source-array snapshot and broader descriptor synchronization contracts remain open. |

AArch64 BCM2712/RP1 global mapping caller reconciliation (2026-10-24; OD922 cross-check, no new EK): reread `krnMMUMap()`/`krnMMUUnmap()` and the map-range alignment/walk (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/mmu.c:180-355`), then traced the selected BCM2712 PCI and RP1 PCI methods. Both DMA allocators reject zero size, round to 4 KiB, return a 4 KiB-aligned address, map that page-rounded span, and remap the same span cacheable before freeing. The BCM2712 BAR mapper validates that the initial PCI address is within its single hardware-derived outbound window, translates it by the window offset, then maps the supplied length; it does not check that the full length stays within the window. Its selected callers include MSI-X table setup (`driverclass.c:461-515`) and RP1's 4 MiB BAR1 setup (`rp1_init.c:174-198`); neither caller's reviewed checks prove a span crossing the outbound-window end. Keep the length/window boundary conditional under Other Drivers OD922, not as a new EK. Correction to the prior note: `rp1_init.c` gets the real RP1 endpoint's bridge-driver pointer and calls that driver's `MapPCI` for its 4 MiB BAR1; the selected BCM2712 bridge method translates the BAR bus address through the hardware-derived outbound window (`driverclass.c:245-265`; `pcie2712_init.c:762-806`). The selected cause vector invokes the HostLib `raise(SIGUSR2)` (`arch/all-unix/kernel/cause.c:12-18`); POSIX `raise()` directs the signal to the calling thread and waits for a handler it invokes to return ([Linux man-pages `raise(3)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/raise.3.html)). Startup installs the SIGUSR2 `core_IRQ` handler, removes SIGUSR2 from the interrupt-block mask, and unblocks it (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel.c:282-288,310-340`); the handler runs the IRQ chain and `core_ExitInterrupt()`, which dispatches pending soft interrupts before scheduling (`kernel.c:125-180`; `kernel_intr.c:24-55`). This ordinary Enable path therefore does not rely on process-directed signal selection among host threads; the separate Darwin forwarding code handles process-directed timer signals. No lost-softint or cross-thread dispatch defect was established. External direct `KrnCause` callers, non-POSIX host behavior, HostLib raise failure, and actual scheduling remain untested and open. No signal, host process, or build was run; source-only.

Unix SAD descriptor-state follow-up (EK10330): re-read `KrnObtainInput`, `KrnReleaseInput`, the complete `InternalDebug` entry/quit path and Unix kernel manifest selection. The Unix acquire path adds `O_NONBLOCK` to stderr but stores no prior value; the normal quit path calls release, which clears the flag unconditionally. A stderr descriptor that was already nonblocking therefore exits the debugger in blocking mode; aliases of the same open file description share that status. The finding is limited to Unix-hosted builds with initially nonblocking stderr and a normal SAD exit. No host descriptor or debugger session was changed.

This conditionally exposes a false processor count/topology; no matching in-tree DTB was found. EK771 is now detailed: the broad `memory` prefix ignores node type/status, and recorded regions are later identity-mapped and published as allocator banks when eligible; disabled banks or large memory-controller apertures remain conditional and no matching in-tree node was found. EK794 follows a separate valid multi-bank layout: the parser selects the largest retained bank (up to eight regions), but startup pairs its end with `__kernel_end` for one bootstrap MemHeader. If that bank lies above the fixed kernel bank, the range includes the gap and the later bank loop treats it as already covered; if its end is below the kernel end, unsigned `IPTR` subtraction wraps and feeds an oversized size into header construction. The target has no matching board FDT in-tree, so both remain conditional topology cases. EK781 also follows short root cell-count property reads into a possible false memory-map fallback; EK772 details unvalidated root cell counts overflowing the early parser `reg` tuple-width calculation and make `read_cells` walk past the property/DTB before startup fallbacks; this requires a malformed DTB. Other width mismatches can also decode the tuple incorrectly; no matching board DTB is present in-tree. The zero-width trigger is a malformed DTB; other topology and malformed-DTB contracts remain pending. Low-memory handler retry cursor recheck (2026-10-12; EK8818, no new candidate): `AllocMem` initializes `cmhs_CurNode` to the list head once before its retry loop (`rom/exec/allocmem.c:108-116`). `checkMemHandlers` assigns the current handler to that cursor before invoking it, retains that cursor when the callback returns `MEM_TRY_AGAIN`, and restarts from it on the next allocation attempt (`rom/exec/memory.c:1329-1348`). `RemMemHandler` recursively acquires `LowMemSem`, then `Remove` only relinks predecessor/successor and leaves the removed node's own links unchanged (`remmemhandler.c:46-52`; `remove.c:55-63`). So a callback that removes/frees itself and requests a retry leaves the next pass starting from its detached node; the list semaphore excludes external concurrent mutation but permits callback self-removal. None of the three checked built-in producers demonstrates that exact combination (diskfont returns `MEM_ALL_DONE`, log.resource returns `MEM_DID_NOTHING`, LDDemon stays registered). The conditional caller contract and allocation-failure trigger remain those in EK8818; no handler or failed allocation was run.

Low-memory handler lifetime finding recheck (2026-10-13; EK34 retained, no scope change): reread `AllocMem`'s cursor snapshot and failed-allocation branch alongside `checkMemHandlers`, `RemMemHandler`, and the selected diskfont library's registration/expunge callbacks (`rom/exec/allocmem.c:105-116`; `rom/exec/memory.c:1313-1334`; `rom/exec/remmemhandler.c:46-52`; `workbench/libs/diskfont/diskfont_init.c:49-55,65-77`). The list semaphore is acquired only after the cursor is captured and the failed allocation returns; diskfont unregisters its embedded handler during generated expunge before its base storage can be freed. This preserves EK34's concrete selected-owner lifetime trigger. The separate callback self-removal plus `MEM_TRY_AGAIN` condition remains EK8818 and is not established by the three built-in handlers. No allocator or expunge race was induced.

Low-memory handler selected-owner rollback and retry audit (2026-10-13; no additional finding): checked all three maintained C registrations and callback returns against allocator retry semantics. Diskfont unregisters in library expunge and its callback returns `MEM_ALL_DONE`; log.resource returns `MEM_DID_NOTHING`, but its init failure after registration bypasses `RemMemHandler` and frees its base through `_set_libinit` rollback (`compiler/autoinit/functions.c:42-69`; generated caller in `tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1156-1180`), as already detailed by EK8782. LDDemon is in the resident Exec base, remains registered, and returns `MEM_TRY_AGAIN` only after a library/device was successfully removed; the retained cursor therefore still names live resident handler storage on the next allocation retry (`rom/lddemon/lddemon.c:682-779,831-916`). None of these selected callbacks demonstrates EK8818's self-removal/freed-successor condition. External callback clients and allocation-retry behavior remain unverified; no failure was induced.

<a id="deleteiorequest-size-width-ek10365"></a>
`CreateIORequest()`/`DeleteIORequest()` size-width pass (EK10365 added; 2026-11-01; no body/path/LOC credit): re-read both complete Exec implementations and the public `Message` layout. `CreateIORequest()` accepts `ULONG size`, allocates it, then assigns it to `UWORD mn_Length`; `DeleteIORequest()` forwards that field to `FreeMem()`, whose zero-size guard returns before releasing the pointer. A caller-supplied size of 65,536 therefore leaks a successfully allocated block on the ordinary delete path. A source search across selected C/assembly trees found no maintained creator passing an oversized constant; this remains scoped to a public caller requesting a large custom request. Rechecked the existing exact 65,536/65,537-byte boundary candidates and did not count partial/wrong-size allocator behavior beyond this directly established zero-size path. The complete wider deletion ownership/completion audit remains open. No allocator operation, build, or runtime behavior was exercised; source-only.

Selected PC i8042 keyboard setup deletes its timer reply port in the worker on request/open/reset failures, after finishing its synchronous timer operations; the mouse worker deletes the port on request/open failures but retains it with the opened timer on later success or reset failure (OD982). | `rom/exec/doresetcallbacks.c` | Full body and all checked-in shutdown/reboot call sites reconciled; platform-runtime behavior pending | Shutdown loop, support-task timeout path, platform callers and concurrent reset-list mutation checked; EK675 covers silent callback skip if `NewCreateTask` fails, including the selected PC single-action reboot falling through to power-off; EK59 details stale saved-next traversal if another task removes the next callback while this path waits for its support task; the removed node retains its link fields, so the walker can invoke an unregistered callback, and freeing its containing owner can turn the next iteration into a stale read/call. The selected generic, AArch64 and Unix `ShutdownA` wrappers all reach this function, while the `KrnIsSuper()` branch invokes callbacks directly with interrupts disabled. Only its non-supervisor branch allocates a completion signal, starts support tasks, and uses timer.device; EK873 and EK8992 are now explicitly scoped to that branch. On SMP, NewAddTask makes a created handler TS_READY before NewCreateTask returns (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:30-43,311-327`), and another eligible CPU can take it from the shared ready list (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:299-323`); InitETask inherits the creator's affinity mask (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:130-165`). A short handler can therefore clear the shared ResetCallbackTask slot before the launcher assigns it, leaving a stale pointer until the next reset-list iteration. No distinct observable failure from that short-completion sequence is established, so it is not a separate candidate; the timed-out late-completion sequence remains EK873. Rechecked timer-signal reuse: Wait clears the returned timer bit; on handler-completion wake the code aborts/WaitIOs the timer and explicitly clears any late timer signal with SetSignal before the next callback. Thus no additional stale-timer-bit finding is retained. `WaitIO` only removes a replied request and does not itself clear a signal; the explicit reset-path clear matters. This launcher times out a non-completing support task when timer.device is available, so GD2239 does not by itself prove that hardware reset stops; EK8992 still covers loss of that timeout when timer setup fails. Remaining platform shutdown and task-lifetime contracts pending. |

| `rom/exec/waitport.c` | Full 39-code-line body read; SMP list-lock/sleep/recheck and borrowed-head return traced; all 17 maintained direct-return consumers checked; ordinary wait-then-dequeue caller/lifecycle inventory remains open | Rechecked the loop and returned list head against `GetMsg`, `PutMsg`, and `ReplyMsg`. A concurrent second consumer could remove that head before the caller uses it, but the public contract and selected caller patterns reviewed here do not establish an independent Exec defect. The BTSerial opener/worker same-port race is OD3366 in Other Drivers: its issue is the caller waiting on the unit input port after `ReplyMsg` targets the caller-provided reply port, not a defect in WaitPort itself. AsyncIO `AS_WaitPacket` still uses WaitPort followed by an unlocked `Remove` and relies on one outstanding packet; its selected Read/Write/Seek/Close paths funnel through the same `af_PacketPending` path. The reviewed filesystem handler and USB startup uses wait on private/owned ports; ConClip shutdown is separately covered by EK9529. The optional Workbench VMM `PD_FILE` caller waits on its private `MultiPagePort` then dequeues one reply (`pageio.c:617-633`). Its only producer is `WriteMultiplePages()`, reached through `FlushCache()` from either `AllocPageOnDisk()` in the serialized `PageHandler` fault loop or `NewCache()` while that same task handles a VMM message (`cache.c:125-150,181-218,281-303`; `pagehandler.c:513-530,550-566`). EK614 follows the PC map builder's header-only acceptance check; both PC startups use that builder. The hosted bootstrap assigns whole-MiB lengths to its ordinary first RAM map and optional upper map for valid positive memory settings (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:303-324`); the selected MinGW startup passes the first map's `len` directly (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_startup.c:116-139`), so these hosted normal paths do not supply EK614's tiny fragment. Negative, zero or overflowing user memory settings need separate bootstrap validation. The selected m68k caller rejects regions under 64 KiB (`arch/m68k-amiga/boot/start.c:344-347`), and RISC-V OpenSBI's extra-bank loop requires at least 1 MiB (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:986-996`). EK9234 covers the conditional PPC Sam440 first-header size wrap when the Parthenope kernel-plus-module cursor reaches 16 MiB; default built-image reachability remains unverified. Its later private header still needs upstream validation. Native ARM and SiFive U's apparent plain-header calls are inside `#if (0)` branches (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_startup.c:279-289`; `arch/riscv-native/sifive_u/kernel/kernel_startup.c:188-199`); their selected startup uses `krnCreateTLSFMemHeader`, so this classic constructor is not reached there. `krnCreateROMHeader` takes an inclusive last address and stores `mh_Upper = end + 1`. CE boot passes `LoadKernel`'s advanced `ptr_ro`, which is likewise exclusive (`arch/arm-native/ceboot/bootstrap.c:184,200-202`; `bootstrap/elfloader.c:740-741`). These informational headers cover one byte beyond the image. `FindMem` walks the priority-sorted list and returns an ordinary RAM header first where one covers that byte (`rom/exec/memory.c:25-62`), so no separate ordinary misclassification is credited from this overlap alone. Hosted Unix/MinGW bootstrap explicitly sets the high tag to `ro_addr + ro_size - 1` (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:382-383`), matching the helper's inclusive contract; PPC Sam440's selected reserved-region callers explicitly subtract one too. WaitForPort break-during-reply SMP cross-check (EK358 expanded; 2026-11-01; no body/path/LOC credit): re-read the timer interrupt producer, `ReplyMsg()`/`InternalPutMsg()`, and the command's break-first cleanup branch. This is an additional timing trigger for EK358's existing missing AbortIO/WaitIO cleanup root cause, not a separate finding. On uniprocessor builds, task cleanup cannot run until the interrupt returns, so this specific overlap is excluded; the queued-request case remains. No build, command, interrupt, or SMP interleaving was run; source-only.

Asyncio zero-buffer read follow-up: `workbench/libs/asyncio/src/OpenAsyncFH.c:61-83,120-124,153-182` and `ReadAsync.c:45-65` were checked together with `SendPacket.c:14-18` and `WaitPacket.c:17-65`. A zero buffer posts a zero-length read at open; a zero-byte completion makes a later positive-length read return zero without consuming file data. EK462 now records this read effect alongside the previously established zero-buffer write loop. The exported API documentation recommends 8192 bytes but states no minimum (`workbench/libs/asyncio/asyncio.doc:150-163`). No selected in-tree read caller supplying zero was found; filesystem-specific zero-length packet handling remains open.

Asyncio signed-length follow-up: the complete `ReadAsync.c` and `PeekAsync.c` bodies were reread against their public signed `LONG` arguments and Exec `CopyMem` (`rom/exec/copymem.c:15-18,60-90`). A negative count reaches CopyMem in either helper; EK860 records this invalid public-input case, with no selected negative caller established. Repository C/H callers found by searching `ReadAsync(` and `PeekAsync(` pass positive one-byte constants in the local wrappers; no selected negative-length caller was established. Other architecture-specific copy paths and external-client contracts remain open.

Asyncio zero-length peek follow-up: `PeekAsync.c:38-56` was checked against `ReadAsync.c:45-86` and the read-mode prefetch in `OpenAsyncFH.c:162-183`. With an empty current buffer, `PeekAsync(file, ..., 0)` calls `ReadAsync(..., 1)` and can wait for the outstanding packet before it performs a zero-length copy (EK857). A direct `ReadAsync(..., 0)` skips that wait. The exported documentation does not require a positive peek length, but no selected in-tree caller of `PeekAsync` was found; slow-source behavior was inferred and not run.

Asyncio write-wrapper follow-up: full `WriteCharAsync.c` and `WriteLineAsync.c` bodies were reread against `WriteAsync.c:38-76`. They forward their values to the shared write routine, whose normal-handler path also passes a negative signed `numBytes` to `CopyMem`; EK860 covers this public invalid-input case across reads, peeks and writes. This is a public invalid-input case with no selected in-tree negative-count caller. The wrappers add no separate valid-input finding on the checked paths; remaining filesystem and external-caller contracts stay open.

Asyncio line-error follow-up: full `FGetsLenAsync.c` and `ReadLineAsync.c` bodies were reread against the documented `ReadLineAsync` result contract (`workbench/libs/asyncio/asyncio.doc:294-328`) and `ReadAsync.c:45-65`. `FGetsLenAsync.c:95-121` coalesces a refill result of `-1` with EOF, setting a zero or partial positive length; `ReadLineAsync` exposes that as zero or partial success (EK855). EK854 covers the distinct too-small-buffer path where the length output is never assigned. No selected in-tree line-reader caller or injected filesystem error was established.

VMM bitmap/cache caller follow-up: `bitmap.c:19-56,61-113,247-333` and `cache.c:24-67,125-176` were rechecked against the page-handler initialization/cleanup path (`pagehandler.c:114-176,181-223,543-554`) and Exec `FreeMem`'s null guard (`rom/exec/freemem.c:60-75`). If bitmap setup succeeds but the write-cache allocation fails, the page handler calls `Cleanup_PageHandler`, which runs `KillCache`; `FreeMem(NULL, BufSize)` is a no-op and the bitmap allocation is freed. No separate leak or null-free candidate is retained for that failure. Exhausted backing slots, sparse cache flushes, resize ownership and optional VMM target viability still require checks.

VMM capacity/configuration follow-up: `VM_Manager_Init.c:742-750` caps exposed virtual memory against page-file size minus an estimated table allowance; `cache.c:30-52,125-156` reserves cache slots in the same bitmap. `AllocSlotNextTo` returns slot 0 in a non-debug no-free-bit case, but the normal exhaustion trigger is not established after capacity accounting, and the selected optional AROS VMM startup is already blocked by EK9906. Bitmap mutation is serialized in PageHandler: `AllocNewCache` only allocates and posts a message, while `NewCache` performs map changes in the receiver. No active swap-full or bitmap-race candidate is counted. A direct configuration caller was established instead: the optional preferences app's 60-character partition-name gadget and `MUI/config.c:435-444` writer can produce a valid saved name longer than the handler's 40-byte globals; `config.c:127-131` copies it into both. EK447 was extended to this partition-backed path. Partition/device startup and target build viability remain open.

EK480 platform recheck: the selected PC SMP dispatcher removes a task from Ready under its own list lock and releases that lock before `SET_THIS_TASK` inserts it into Running under the separate Running lock (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:304-321,348-355`; `arch/all-pc/exec/exec_platform.h:295-305`). PC switch-out removes Running first and later inserts Ready (`kernel_scheduler.c:205-213,248-261`). This supplies the same false-absence windows already documented for ARM SMP in `FindTaskByPID`, `Exec_CheckTask` and `FindTask(name)`; EK480 now names both selected SMP scheduler families. `SetTaskPri` has a separate task lock and ready-list reorder (`rom/exec/settaskpri.c:72-112`), so its priority update was not used as evidence of an unlocked scheduler transition. Other platform variants and external lookup callers remain open.
CPU-mask cross-target follow-up: the generic `rom/kernel/{alloccpumask,freecpumask,clearcpumask,cpuinmask}.c` stubs were compared with the selected `arch/all-pc/kernel` and native ARM32/AArch64 overrides of those four functions, plus `arch/all-pc/kernel/apic.c:115-165` and `rom/task/SetTaskAffinity.c:68-143`. PC allocates a word count from APIC CPU count; native ARM targets use one word under their four-core platform assumption. Selected setters and clear/free routines recognize the `TASKAFFINITY_ANY` sentinel; PC treats a null mask as boot-CPU-only, while native ARM treats null as unrestricted. Existing low-memory affinity findings and the stale `QueryTaskTagList(TaskTag_CPUAffinity)` result already cover the concrete differences found here. `SetTaskAffinity` validates that a non-ANY input names an online CPU and copies bits into task-owned storage; no additional ordinary selected-caller defect was established by this pass. Dynamic APIC CPU-count changes after allocation, ARM CPU IDs beyond the one-word platform limit, and external direct mask callers remain unverified.
NewCreateTaskA message-port output follow-up: a repository search located the visible `TASKTAG_TASKMSGPORT` C callers, and the late `NewAddTask`-failure path was rechecked against `newcreatetaska.c:218-272`. The helper publishes the newly allocated port before `NewAddTask` succeeds and does not clear it when freeing that allocation; this remains the existing EK06 candidate. `rom/log/log.c:304-312` uses the published port as its success criterion, and selected PC serial logging also ignores the returned task, as already documented. The checked SCSI daemon/bus, console, input, narrator, speech, usb2otg, CD and CD32 MPEG callers test the task result before proceeding; no new stale-port use was established from those paths. SCSI bus startup's separate semaphore behavior and individual failed-init cleanup remain open. No task-allocation failure was run.
Exec service startup follow-up: `rom/exec/exec_init.c:303-352` and the PPC CHRP boot variant `arch/ppc-chrp/exec/exec_init.c:393-413` both test the housekeeper `NewCreateTask` return rather than trusting its early `TASKTAG_TASKMSGPORT` output, so they do not add a selected stale-port-use path to EK06. The generic initializer does not check the later Guru-task creation result, but `SupervisorAlertTask` alone publishes `SAT.sat_Task` and `sat_IsAvailable` on startup (`rom/exec/supervisoralert.c:30-37`); `Exec_SystemAlert` takes its kernel-display fallback while that availability flag is false (`rom/exec/systemalert.c:63-75`). Thus a failed Guru-task allocation reduces alert handling to the fallback instead of establishing an unchecked-null signal or lost alert. No separate finding is credited; platform alert-display behavior and startup memory pressure remain untested.
KrnStatMemoryA aggregate-contract follow-up: `rom/kernel/statmemory.c:20-123`, `rom/kernel/mm_linear.c:455-568`, the public `KMS_*` definitions (`compiler/include/aros/kernel.h:123-133`), and the repository C call sites were compared. The documented page-size result is a `ULONG`, and the implementation writes exactly that type; all other documented results are `IPTR` and start at zero before the selected MMU block-map walk. The selected production caller in `rom/exec/addresource.c:89` asks only for page size, taking the early return without touching any MemHeader; the unselected allocator test source also requests only page size (`developer/debug/test/kernel/mmakefile.src:5-11` excludes it). No aggregate-statistics use by a selected production caller was found, so traversal races and map accounting remain public/external-caller questions rather than newly credited runtime findings. Unknown tag IDs are zeroed as `IPTR` per the generic branch, but the source documents no output type for unknown tags; no selected unknown-tag call establishes an ordinary buffer-width defect.
EK541 detailed recheck: AArch64 Raspberry Pi SMP boot attempts CPU IDs 1-3 separately and continues after a refused PSCI start (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:359-410`); each started core marks its numbered bit (`kernel_cpu.c:136-155,323-330`). The platform init hook invokes this startup before Exec idle-task init (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_init.c:100-124`; `arch/aarch64-native/exec/platform_init.c:39-96,233`). `getcpucount.c:13-22` returns bit population, while Exec idle-task creation and `rom/task/SetTaskAffinity.c:83-108` treat the count as a dense ID range. CPU 1 refused and CPU 2 started yields count two but registered IDs 0 and 2: the idle task is assigned to unavailable CPU 1, CPU 2 has no corresponding idle-task entry, CPU-2-only affinity is rejected, and `getsystemattr.c:34-45` reports zero load when its idle-task entry is missing. The ARM32 BCM2708 path waits on each ID before trying the next and was not shown to have the same skip-and-continue trigger. No PSCI failure or runtime scheduling was reproduced. Detailed report entry restored as `AROS-exec-kernel.md#ek541`, with the AROS index linked to it.
EK541 ARM32 boundary recheck: `arch/arm-native/kernel/platform_bcm2708.c:115-161` wakes CPU IDs 1-3 in order, but waits on the startup lock without a timeout before attempting the next ID. A CPU that never reports does not produce the AArch64 example of skipping ID 1 and successfully starting ID 2 through this selected ARM32 path; it stalls the boot loop instead. `arch/arm-native/kernel/getcpucount.c:13-24` also returns affinity-mask population and `arch/arm-native/exec/platform_init.c:37-98` uses it as a dense-ID bound, but the concrete sparse-start trigger established for EK541 is AArch64's PSCI refusal/continue branch, not ARM32's strict sequence. Other ARM32 platform initializers and post-registration failure handling remain open.
Reset-callback caller cross-check: searched direct `AddResetCallback`/`RemResetCallback` uses across selected architecture and driver trees. The AROS Envy24 per-card unload lifetime is already OD303 in the other-drivers report; EMU10kx's similar static callback body is gated by `__AMIGAOS4__`, so it is not an AROS-path duplicate. Reset-callback caller refinement: CMI8738's actual `AddResetHandler` definition and call are both inside `!__AROS__` guards (`workbench/devs/AHI/Drivers/CMI8738/misc.c:311-315,613-644`), so it is not a selected AROS reset-list producer. Display reset-callback caller refinement: native VGA and AArch64 Raspberry Pi framebuffer HIDDs register only after successful display construction, but coerce partial object disposal when display construction fails, and their disposers remove the unregistered node; the AArch64 Raspberry Pi fbgfx partial-dispose path is now detailed as GD4111 (`arch/aarch64-raspi/hidd/fbgfx/fbgfx_hiddclass.c:77-105`); native VGA partial-dispose behavior remains referenced by historical GD95 (`arch/all-native/hidd/vgagfx/vgagfx_hiddclass.c:102-126`). Linux framebuffer registers after successful display construction and removes its callback on normal object disposal (`arch/all-linux/hidd/linuxfb/linuxfbgfx_hiddclass.c:125-160`); its failed-display path never disposes the graphics object, already GD134, and normal disposal leaves the console descriptor open, already GD135. No additional generic Exec callback-lifetime finding is credited from these three display HIDDs. Remaining display modules and unload-versus-shutdown concurrency stay open under EK59.

The PC APIC callback is embedded in platform data and registered from CPU-0 timer setup (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic_ia32.c:916-928`); that data remains a resident kernel owner. Selected Workbench C command caller follow-up: `workbench/c/mmakefile.src` selects `DevList.c` in FILES and `Debug.c` in SH_FILES. Both complete bodies were read. DevList snapshots the Exec device list under Forbid or, on SMP when execlock.resource is present, a read lock; its backward name-copy guard reserves the next two `struct dev` slots before it advances the record pointer. The local buffer layout therefore does not establish an overflow from the pre-copy field writes. AddDevice takes the corresponding write lock. Device removal, absent-resource SMP startup, and third-party list producers remain open; no new candidate is credited from these two commands.

Audio-device CheckIO/WaitIO caller follow-up: `workbench/devs/audio/audio_commands.c:371-385,1048-1095` skips `WaitIO` on a completed AHI request, thereby leaving its reply-port node queued; the audio slave can submit that request again from a channel write before draining the old reply. This is a caller error recorded as other-driver OD1879, not a new defect in Exec's documented CheckIO/WaitIO operations. The selected audio device also uses a shared reply port for four requests, relevant to EK8819's separate unlocked removal path. Source-only; no timing sequence was run.
EK673 caller/spec refinement: the selected `CreateSegList` caller constructs a RISC-V `FullJumpVec` and calls `CacheClearE(..., CACRF_ClearI | CACRF_ClearD)`; the preceding `fence rw,rw` and SBI remote FENCE.I satisfy the instruction-visibility sequence, so the executable-code subclaim is withdrawn ([Zifencei](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/zifencei.html), [SBI RFENCE](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/sbi/ext-rfence.html)). The remaining EK673 candidate is DMA: `cpu_Init` installs Zicbom `CachePreDMA`/`CachePostDMA` replacements only when the FDT scan finds Zicbom. Otherwise the selected RISC-V `CachePreDMA` falls back to `CacheClearE(..., CACRF_ClearD)`, while generic `rom/exec/cachepostdma.c` does nothing. The active OpenSBI boot package selects NVMe, VirtIO and PCI xHCI, whose transfer paths call these DMA hooks (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/boot/mmakefile.src`; `rom/devs/nvme/nvme_sgl.c:104, rom/devs/nvme/nvme_intern.h:269-271`; `rom/devs/virtio/virtio_queue.c:182-199`; `rom/usb/pcixhci/xhci_schedule.c:75-88`). On a no-Zicbom system with cached, noncoherent device DMA, writes can reach a device before dirty CPU lines are cleaned, and device-to-memory transfers have no post-DMA invalidation, allowing stale data to be read or written back over device data. The RISC-V CMO extension defines explicit data-cache clean/flush operations for such maintenance ([RISC-V CMO specification](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/unpriv/cmo.html)). This is a conditional hardware/configuration finding; the selected source path is established, but no particular no-Zicbom noncoherent board was run or confirmed. Keep the DMA finding scoped to that condition; coherent devices and Zicbom-enabled systems do not trigger it.
MinGW VBlank timer follow-up (EK674): `arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_startup.c:193-215` publishes a valid caller-supplied `vblank=60` frequency and sends it through `core_init` to timer 0. `host_intr.c:236-245,345-355` requests an integer 16 ms host waitable-timer period, and `kernel_intr.c:78-98` raises one `INTB_VERTB` per delivered timer-0 bit. Selected graphics.library's server increments `VBCounter` and wakes `WaitTOF` clients (`rom/graphics/graphics_init.c:142-153,160-202`; `rom/graphics/waittof.c:50-65`), so that public pacing path is the checked consequence of the non-divisor-rate mismatch. EK8846 covers invalid `vblank=` input and one-shot frequencies, while OD1878 tracks the distinct timer-1 EClock mismatch. The host's observed timing was not measured. Rechecked `TaskSwitcher`'s `MainCtx` reuse while `Sleep_Mode == SLEEP_MODE_ON`: the mode is entered only after a prior loop captured the suspended main-thread context, so the mere skipped `GetThreadContext` in later iterations does not establish an uninitialized-context candidate; context changes outside this selected path remain open.
EK672 timer-0 extension: the same `arch/all-mingw32/kernel/host_intr.c:140-165,182-211` Boolean `PendingInts` slot that loses repeated timer-1 signals also loses repeated timer-0 signals observed while AROS IRQs are disabled. Host `core_init` starts timer 0 (`:345-355`), and `arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_intr.c:91-94` emits only one `INTB_VERTB` for its set byte on resumption. Graphics.library's VBlank server increments `VBCounter` once per dispatch (`rom/graphics/graphics_init.c:160-202`), so the counter can undercount host VBlank notifications. A `WaitTOF` waiter still receives one wake when dispatch resumes; no claim of an extra post-resumption stall is credited. The same underlying queue defect stays EK672, while EK674 concerns timer 0's independent requested-period truncation. No Windows timing sequence was run.
Audio shared-reply-port caller follow-up (OD4088 cross-reference corrected, 2026-10-23): `workbench/devs/audio/audio_commands.c:2261-2270,2325-2334` uses `Wait(1 << mp_SigBit)` as an internal worker acknowledgement and may `ReplyMsg` its own still-queued command if the reply-port bit is already set. Exec `PutMsg` signals per port, without identifying a particular request (`rom/exec/putmsg.c:83-119`); its `WaitIO` instead loops on the specified request's completion state (`rom/exec/waitio.c:57-78`). This is the existing Other Drivers finding OD4088, not a new Exec signal or port contract defect. No shared-port timing was run.
Task-storage snapshot failure cross-check: `SaveTaskStorage` returns null when it cannot allocate a copy of the current slot array (`rom/task/SaveTaskStorage.c:51-73`). `RestoreTaskStorage` frees the current array and installs its handle, including null (`rom/task/RestoreTaskStorage.c:47-69`). The `NewStackSwap` wrapper calls the former, invokes the old vector, then calls the latter without checking the saved handle (`rom/task/task_execfuncs.c:195-225`), so enabling that wrapper would clear the current task's storage after a failed snapshot. The selected `task_init.c:79-81` keeps the wrapper's `SetFunction` under `#if (0)`, and a repository C call search found no other direct caller of either snapshot API. No default-build finding is credited from this wrapper sequence; external task.resource clients and a future enabled wrapper remain open. No allocation failure or stack swap was run.
EK674 timer.device boundary check: the selected MinGW timer initializer registers timer 1 for EClock ticks and separately registers a VBlank server (`arch/all-mingw32/timer/timer_init.c:36-52,64-74,100-113`; `rom/timer/timervblank.c:15-39`). The timer-1 callback advances `tb_CurrentTime` and `tb_Elapsed`, while `TimerProcessVBlank` checks queued `UNIT_VBLANK`/`UNIT_WAITUNTIL` requests against those counters (`rom/timer/lowlevel.c:343-395`). The generic `EClockUpdate` is empty on this target (`rom/timer/ticks.c:9-16`). Thus timer-0's 16 ms truncation produces extra VBlank notifications and faster graphics `VBCounter`/`WaitTOF` pacing as EK674 says, but this check does not prove timer.device elapsed time or `UNIT_VBLANK` deadlines run 4.17% fast: their clock accumulation is driven by timer 1. Timer-1 non-divisor behavior is tracked separately by OD1878. No Windows timers were run.
Exec housekeeper requeue ordering check: self-`RemTask` enters `Forbid` before setting `TS_REMOVED`, publishing its task node to `ServicePort`, and finally setting `TS_INVALID` before `KrnDispatch` (`rom/exec/remtask.c:70-88,130-164`). It disables local interrupts before it resets forbid nesting, so on a single CPU the higher-priority housekeeper cannot run in the published-but-removed interval; its `TS_REMOVED` requeue loop does not establish a same-CPU self-exit deadlock. On SMP another CPU may dequeue and immediately requeue while the departing CPU continues, causing transient work until the state changes; no enduring selected failure was established from that loop alone. EK807 (former EK659) separately covers premature free after the later `TS_INVALID` store on another CPU. No scheduling sequence was run.

### m68k Amiga SetPatch module and command inventory

The active `workbench-c-m68k` aggregate names both SetPatch commands, and the ordinary SetPatch command depends on the explicit `kernel-setpatch` link library (`arch/m68k-amiga/c/mmakefile.src:14-33`; `arch/m68k-amiga/setpatch/mmakefile.src:6-11`). These nine previously absent local source, definition and manifest files have now been added to the ledger. The module declares `noexpunge`, so its two embedded public ports, public semaphore and patched FindSemaphore vector retain their owner for the module lifetime. External patch-entry clients and actual m68k runtime behavior remain open.
